# Walter Murch — The Rule of Six

**Source work:** Murch, W., *In the Blink of an Eye: A Perspective on Film Editing* (Silman-James Press, 1995), pp. 17–20
**Evidence tag: 🟠**

**Source opened (in the harvest):** a verbatim quotation of the book itself, pp. 17–20 of
Murch, W., *In the Blink of an Eye: A Perspective on Film Editing* (Silman-James Press,
1995), reproduced on a UC Berkeley iSchool course blog. The weights were cross-checked
against several independent secondary summaries (PremiumBeat, Artlist, FilmDaft — search
results) and all agree exactly, but the list below is from the book text itself.

## (a) Core finding — the six criteria, in Murch's priority order, with his weights
An ideal cut satisfies all six at once; when they conflict, sacrifice **from the bottom
up**, never give up a higher criterion for a lower one:

| # | Criterion | Weight | Murch's own test |
|---|-----------|--------|------------------|
| 1 | **Emotion** | **51%** | Is it true to the emotion of the moment? ("How do you want the audience to feel?") |
| 2 | **Story** | 23% | Does it advance the story? |
| 3 | **Rhythm** | 10% | Does it occur at a moment that is rhythmically interesting and "right"? |
| 4 | **Eye-trace** | 7% | Does it acknowledge the location and movement of the audience's focus of interest within the frame? |
| 5 | **Two-dimensional plane of screen** | 5% | Does it respect "planarity" — the grammar of 3-D transposed to 2-D (stage line, screen direction)? |
| 6 | **Three-dimensional space of action** | 4% | Does it respect the 3-D continuity of the actual space (where people really are relative to each other)? |

Emotion alone (51%) is worth more than the other five combined; the top two (emotion +
story = 74%) dwarf the bottom four. Murch's mechanism: if the higher criteria are right,
the audience tends to be *unaware of* problems with the lower ones — but not vice versa
(perfect spatial continuity cannot rescue a cut that fails emotion). He also notes the
top three — emotion, story, rhythm — are bound together "like the bonds between protons
and neutrons", far tighter than the connections lower down.

## (b) Evidence base
One master editor's distilled craft experience (Murch edited *The Conversation*,
*Apocalypse Now*, *The Godfather* films). There are **no experiments** behind the Rule of
Six, and Murch says so himself in the quoted text: the percentages are "slightly
tongue-in-cheek, but not completely" — they encode a priority order, not a measurement.
Two partial cross-validations from the same harvest are worth noting: his #4 criterion,
eye-trace, is exactly what Tim Smith's eye-tracking later measured (🟢, see
science_tim_smith.md), and his bottom ranking of literal spatial continuity matches the
"edit blindness" observation that viewers barely register spatial/continuity details
when attention is engaged (reported in secondary summaries; see the Smith file's note).

## (c) Tag: 🟠
Reason: by the author's own admission the weights are a pedagogical device from one
editor's intuition — supremely influential craft wisdom, but opinion, not evidence.
(The *ordering* may deserve promotion later if the user's own tests confirm it; the
numbers themselves should never be treated as measured.)

## (d) Editing rules it converts into
- **R-MUR-1 (conflict order — the engine's tie-breaker):** IF two candidate cuts conflict,
  THEN score them in this order and let the higher criterion win: Emotion > Story >
  Rhythm > Eye-trace > 2-D plane > 3-D space. Sacrifice from the bottom up. 🟠
- **R-MUR-2 (emotion veto):** IF a cut is technically perfect (continuity, screen
  direction, rhythm all clean) but it breaks the emotion of the moment, THEN reject the
  cut — no lower-criterion score can compensate. 🟠
- **R-MUR-3 (continuity is expendable):** IF preserving 3-D spatial continuity forces a
  cut that weakens emotion or stalls the story, THEN break the continuity — audiences
  demonstrably forgive spatial jumps when emotion and story hold. 🟠 (with 🟢-leaning
  support from Smith's attention findings)
- **R-MUR-4 (aim for all six):** IF a cut satisfying all six exists, THEN take it —
  "never accept less when more is available"; the hierarchy is only for forced trade-offs.
  🟠

**Note for the user's system:** Murch's order is a close cousin of the user's own
priority — **Kahani > Samajh aana > Rhythm > Style/Effect** — with one difference worth
deciding deliberately: Murch puts *emotion* (51%) strictly above *story* (23%), while
the user's "Kahani" bundles the two together.
